description_full: VAT Group AG, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the development, manufacture, and sale of vacuum and gas inlet valves, multi-valve modules, motion components, and edge-welded metal bellows. It operates in two segments, Valves and Global Service. The Valves segment offers vacuum valves for the semiconductor, displays, photovoltaics, and vacuum coating industries, as well as for the industrial and research sectors. The Global Service segment provides spare parts, repairs, and upgrades, as well as support services. The company offers vacuum isolation, gate, angle, inline, check, cylinder, and all-metal valves; vacuum pendulum and butterfly valves; 3 position, multi-value, and vacuum control valves; vacuum transfer valves and doors; pressure relief/venting, gas dosing, and fast closing/beam stopper valves; and flange connections, bellows, and vacuum modules. It has operations in Switzerland, rest of Europe, the United States, Japan, Korea, Singapore, China, rest of Asia, and internationally. VAT Group AG was founded in 1965 and is headquartered in Solothurn, Switzerland.

financial_summary: VAT Group AG is a large-cap industrials business with a $19.2B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are contracting by -2.6pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 8% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 65% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $275M in free cash flow — roughly 22 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.40× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 74× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 10% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 56% and a beta of 0.57, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.55 vs 5y 0.31), so read it loosely.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $123 (margin of safety -392%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $99.06 to $159 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.3x net debt to EBITDA ($168.2M of cash against $296.2M of debt), with interest covered 74.0x.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.6% over 3 years.

own: Insiders own 10.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 47%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (0.0% in buybacks and 1.5% in dividends).
It pays out 101% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 3,959 employees, each generates about $324K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median.
That works out to $70K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.2M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
